title: Run the weekly flush of an emergency eyewash until the water runs clear, then shut it and cap the heads
instruction: Do the weekly test on the eyewash station.
context: Lab technicians, custodians and safety coordinators learn this weekly check in training and do it without being told the steps (O*NET 19-4021.00, Biological Technicians; 37-2011.00, Janitors and Cleaners; 29-9011.00, Occupational Health and Safety Specialists). OSHA 29 CFR 1910.151(c) requires an eyewash wherever eyes can be splashed with corrosives, and ANSI/ISEA Z358.1 (section 5.5.2) says a plumbed unit is activated weekly to verify the water supply and flush the line. Water standing in the pipe grows bacteria and collects rust and sediment that would be sprayed into an injured eye. So the valve is not just pressed but left open, hands-free on its stay-open valve, until the water runs clear, and then it is shut and the dust covers, which the water pops off, go back on the spray heads to keep airborne dirt out.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A bench-mounted eyewash is fixed on the table, centered at x 31, y 0. A light gray supply housing, 9 x 15 x 4 cm, stands on a brushed steel plate. A round stainless steel bowl, 20 cm across and 5 cm deep, sits on the housing, its rim 9 cm up, with a drain at x 35. Two chrome spray heads, 2.4 cm across, stand in the bowl at x 30.5, y -4.5 and 4.5, their tops 7.4 cm up. Each head wears a yellow plastic dust cover, a cap 2.8 cm across and 0.8 cm thick with a finger tab at its front, hinged at the head's back edge. A cover opens up and back to 110 degrees, past upright, and stays there until pushed forward; past upright it falls shut. A brass supply pipe runs from the housing's right side to a ball valve at x 24, y -15. Its push flag, a steel plate 5 x 4.5 cm with green faces, stands on the valve's vertical stem from 6 to 10.5 cm up. Closed, it points to the robot's right. A quarter turn back, pushed away from the robot, opens the valve, and the flag then lies alongside the bowl. It stays wherever it is left. While the flag is turned 80 degrees or more, water arcs about 3 cm up from both heads, falling back into the bowl 3.5 cm nearer the robot, and pops both covers open. The water runs rust-colored for its first 10 s without a break, then clear.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole run. The valve counts as open with the flag turned 80 degrees or more of its 90, and as shut within 10 degrees of closed. A cover counts as on within 10 degrees of its head. The score is 0 unless the valve stayed open without a break for 240 control steps (12 s at 20 Hz) at some point. So doing nothing, or a short press, scores 0. After such a flush, the end state decides. The valve not shut (water still running, or the flag left part open) scores 0.25. Shut, but a cover not on, scores 0.5. So does a gripper's tool point still within 4.5 cm of the flag's or a cap's center, as if still holding it. Shut, both covers on and hands off scores 1.0 if both arms are also home and still, and 0.9 if not. The arms count as home with each tool point within 3 cm of where it started and still, because they are put back so the workspace is clear for the next person or job. Success is a full score held for 1 s. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0. In a real trial, time the valve's open spell from the video with a stopwatch, then check the flag's angle and both covers.
reset_notes: Turn the flag back to closed and put both covers on. Nothing is used up. In a real trial the unit drains into its bowl, so wipe it dry.
fidelity: About 0.7 scale. The flush is scaled down from the usual 3 minutes (or until clear) to 12 s, and the water runs clear after 10 s. The unit is fixed to the table. No water is simulated: translucent streams, rust-colored and then clear, rise from the heads while the valve is open; they cannot be touched. The water's push on a cover is a torque that opens it while the water flows. The flag turns a quarter turn on a vertical stem and stays where it is left, as a stay-open ball valve does.
